drug_class: FcRn blocker (neonatal Fc receptor antagonist) combined with a spreading agent
purpose: This medication is used to treat adults with a condition called generalized myasthenia gravis, which causes muscle weakness that can make it hard to breathe, swallow, or move. It is also used for a nerve condition called chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) that causes weakness and numbness in the arms and legs. It helps reduce the abnormal antibodies that are causing your immune system to attack your own body.
how_it_works: Your immune system makes proteins called antibodies to fight infections, but in your condition, some of these antibodies are mistakenly attacking your own nerves or muscles. This medicine works by lowering the levels of those harmful antibodies in your blood. The hyaluronidase part of the medicine helps it spread under the skin so it can be absorbed into your body more easily.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include reactions at the injection site such as redness, bruising, pain, or swelling under the skin. You may also experience respiratory infections like the common cold, headache, urinary tract infections, and joint or muscle pain. These side effects are usually mild.
warnings: This medicine lowers certain antibodies, which can increase your risk of getting infections, so let your doctor know right away if you have signs of an infection like fever, chills, or unusual tiredness. It may interfere with allergy skin tests, so make sure any doctor treating you knows you are on this medication. You should not receive live vaccines while on this treatment. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before using this medication.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given as an injection just under the skin, usually in the stomach area. For myasthenia gravis, it is typically given once a week for 4 weeks as a treatment cycle, and cycles may be repeated based on how you are doing. For CIDP, it is usually given every week or every 2 weeks depending on your doctor's plan. Each injection takes only a few minutes and can be given by a healthcare provider or, after training, possibly by yourself at home.
